questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: solve a two-equation system by replacing one variable with its rule
questions.stem: A stall sells two sizes of box, and together the numbers of small and large boxes sold comes to 15 while the rule for large boxes is y equals 3x plus 3, where x counts small boxes. What is the number of small boxes sold? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Substitution replaces the y in the first equation with the rule 3x plus 3, which gives 4x plus 3 equal to 15, so 4x equals 12 and x is 3. The back-substitution confirms the pair: the first equation gives 3 plus 12 which is 15, and the second gives 9 plus 3 which is 12, so both equations are satisfied by 3 and 12. Forgetting to substitute at all, or substituting in the wrong direction, leaves two variables and no way forward.
questions.hint: Replace the y in the first equation with the rule for y, then solve for x.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Building a system with no solution
questions.learningObjective: choose a second equation that makes a system impossible
questions.stem: One equation of a system is 3x plus 5y equals 20. How many solutions does the system have when the second equation is 6x plus 10y equals 40? Report the number of solutions as a whole number, using minus 1 to mean infinitely many.
questions.explanation: Doubling the first equation gives 6x plus 10y equals 40, exactly the second equation, so both describe the same line and every point on it satisfies the system, which is the infinitely many case. Writing the constant as 25 instead keeps the slope and shifts the line, producing parallel lines with no solution at all. The ratio between the coefficients decides the direction, and the ratio of the constants decides the position.
questions.hint: For no solution the two lines must be parallel, so the coefficient ratio must match.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: identify a system whose two lines cross exactly once
questions.stem: A park planner compares the lines 2x plus 3y equal to 12 and 4x plus y equal to 10. How many solutions does this system have, and why?

options.text: Exactly one, since the two lines have different slopes and cross in a single point
None at all, since the two equations were written with different coefficients
options.misconception: believes unequal coefficients make a system impossible rather than solvable

options.text: Infinitely many, since both equations describe straight lines on one grid
options.misconception: assumes every pair of lines on one grid must describe the same points

options.text: Exactly two, one for each equation taken separately on its own
options.misconception: counts solutions per equation rather than points shared by both lines

questions.explanation: The slopes of the two lines are negative two thirds and negative 4, so they are not parallel and not the same line, which means they intersect at exactly one point. A system has one solution precisely when its two lines cross once, and that point satisfies both equations. Equal slopes with equal intercepts would give a shared line and infinitely many solutions, while equal slopes with different intercepts would give none.
questions.hint: Compare the slopes of the two lines before counting any solutions.

questions.stem: A technician graphs two rules and the lines cross at the point where x is 3 and y is 5. What does that crossing tell the technician about the system?

options.text: The pair 3 and 5 satisfies only the equation that was graphed first
options.misconception: believes a crossing belongs to one plotted line rather than to both

options.text: The pair 3 and 5 is the only point that satisfies both equations at once
Every point above the crossing also satisfies both equations together
options.misconception: reads a single crossing as a whole region shared by the two lines

options.text: The system has no solution, because the two lines were drawn on one grid
options.misconception: believes two lines sharing a grid cannot also share a point

questions.explanation: The solution of a system is a point that lies on both lines, and because two non-parallel lines meet once, that point is the only solution. Substituting 3 and 5 into either equation confirms the reading, and the crossing location is not a property of which line was drawn first. A region of shared points would require the two lines to coincide, which is a different case entirely.
questions.hint: Recall that a solution of a system must satisfy every equation in it.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: solve a system by adding equations that cancel one variable
questions.stem: A system reads 5x plus 2y equal to 21 and 3x minus 2y equal to 5. Adding the two equations together gives one value. What is x? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Adding cancels the y terms and leaves 8x equal to 26, so x equal to 26 over 8, which is 3.25. Substituting into the first equation gives 16.25 plus 2y equal to 21, so 2y equal to 4.75 and y equal to 2.375, which also satisfies the second equation. Treating the sum of the right-hand sides, 26, as the value of x instead of 8x is the usual slip here.
questions.hint: Add first to cancel y, then divide by the coefficient of x that remains.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: choose a scaling that makes two coefficients cancel
questions.stem: In the system 3x plus 4y equals 18 and 6x minus 7y equals 3, by what factor must the first equation be multiplied so that the x terms cancel when the equations are added? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The x coefficients are 3 and 6, so doubling the first equation brings its coefficient to 6 and lets the two equations be added to cancel x. Multiplying by 4 would give 12 against 6 and leave x behind, scaling the second equation leaves the 3 unmatched, and adding as they stand combines the coefficients rather than cancelling them. Each factor multiplies every term of its equation, which is why the constant on the right doubles along with the coefficient.
questions.hint: Make the smaller x coefficient into the larger one, then combine the equations.

questions.learningObjective: decide whether to add or subtract to cancel a matched pair
questions.stem: A system is written as 7y minus 2x equal to 9 and minus 2x plus 5y equal to 4. Which operation removes a variable straight away?

options.text: Multiply the first equation by 2 and add, doubling the x coefficient of negative 4
options.misconception: scales needlessly and then chooses the wrong way to combine

options.text: Add the two equations together, since equal x terms cancel when they are combined
options.misconception: believes two like terms vanish when they are added together

options.text: Subtract the second equation from the first, since the terms in x match exactly
Add 2x to both sides of the first equation to make the two x terms alike
options.misconception: alters one equation instead of comparing the pair as they stand

questions.explanation: Both equations carry the same x term of negative 2x, so subtracting one from the other removes it and leaves a single equation in y. Adding the two would instead give negative 4x plus 12y equal to 13, which still carries x, because like terms add rather than cancel. Matching coefficients and choosing subtraction are two separate decisions, and the second follows from the signs once the first is settled.
questions.hint: Compare the coefficients of each variable, then check which way round the subtraction makes them vanish.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: detect a value that fails one equation of a system
questions.stem: A student solves the system x plus y equal to 12 and x minus y equal to 6 by adding the equations to get 2x equal to 18, then reports the answer as x equal to 9 and y equal to 9. What has gone wrong?

options.text: The y value is 18, which is twice the x value that was just found
options.misconception: takes twice the solved value as the second unknown

options.text: The y value must be negative 9, since adding the equations fixed the sign already
options.misconception: carries a sign through an addition that cannot create one

options.text: The y value is 21, from adding the two right-hand sides as well as the x values
options.misconception: adds the constants of both equations together with the unknowns

options.text: The y value must come from an equation, and 12 minus 9 gives 3 rather than 9

questions.explanation: Elimination removes one unknown at a time, so after finding x the second unknown still has to be recovered from one of the original equations, and 12 minus 9 is 3. Reporting 9 for y simply repeats the value already found, which is why the pair must be checked: 9 plus 9 is 18, not 12, and 9 minus 9 is 0, not 6, so the reported answer satisfies neither equation. The check is quick and it is the only way to catch a value that was assumed rather than solved for.
questions.hint: The two unknowns are different quantities, so solve the second one from an equation.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: select the method that suits the shape of a given system
questions.stem: A system is 4x plus 3y equal to 18, together with y equals 6 minus x. Which solving method suits this system best, and why?

options.text: Substitution, because one equation already gives y in terms of x
Elimination, since substitution needs a variable standing entirely alone
options.misconception: requires a bare variable before substitution is allowed

options.text: Substitution, since the coefficients 4 and 3 can never be made to match
options.misconception: believes these two coefficients could never be brought to a common size

options.text: Elimination, since elimination always takes the fewest lines of working
options.misconception: chooses a method by effort rather than by what the system offers

questions.explanation: Substitution is the shortest road when one equation already expresses a variable in terms of the other, and here replacing y by 6 minus x leaves a single equation in x, which is 4x plus 3 of the quantity 6 minus x equal to 18, giving x equal to 0 and then y equal to 6. Elimination is still possible, since the 3 and the negative 1 can be scaled to match, so option C overstates the case. The choice of method is about efficiency, and both routes reach the same pair provided the work is correct.
questions.hint: Look for an equation that already contains only one unknown once the other is named.

Exactly one, because the two coefficients of x differ and must be resolved

The finished rule satisfies the point, since 2 times 3 minus 1 is 5, and that substitution is the check that a different form such as y plus 5 equals 2 times the quantity x plus 3 fails. questions.learningObjective: recognise when a direct subtraction already removes a variable

options.text: 3x plus 2y equal to 7, together with 5x minus 2y equal to 1

3x plus 2y equal to 7, together with 4x minus 7y equal to 1
options.misconception: treats a larger coefficient on one side as though it cancelled a smaller one

questions.explanation: A direct subtraction removes a variable only when its coefficients are equal in size and opposite in sign, and in the first pair the 2y and the negative 2y do exactly that while the 3x terms stay. The other three pairs leave a difference in size behind, so their subtraction produces one equation with both variables still in it and nothing is gained. Scaling is the remedy when the coefficients do not match, and skipping it there is what turns a two-step job into an unsolvable one.

questions.topic: No solution against infinitely many solutions
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference between an impossible system and one that is always true
questions.stem: A solver reports that eliminating a variable from one system left a false statement, and from another left a true statement. Which claim about the two systems is correct?

options.misconception: reads the two leftover statements as meaning the opposite of what they mean

options.text: The false statement system has no solution, and the true statement system has all its line as solutions
Both systems have no solution, because the variable has disappeared in each case
options.misconception: treats the disappearance of a variable as the same as having no solution

options.text: Both systems have infinitely many solutions, because two equations were supplied for each
options.misconception: believes the number of equations alone decides the size of a solution set

When it leaves a true statement, nothing restricts the remaining variable, so the two equations describe the same line and every point on it is a solution. What decides the case is the leftover statement, not the number of equations or the disappearance of the variable itself.

options.misconception: scales one equation and leaves the other unmatched for cancellation

Divide the second equation by 2 so that its y term becomes negative y

options.text: 0.3s equals 0.15s, leaving the 12 litres of water out of the totals
options.misconception: forgets to add the water's volume to the final volume

questions.explanation: The salt does not change during the mixing, so the salt poured in must equal the salt present at the end, and on the way in it is 0.3 of s litres while at the end it is 0.15 of the total volume, which is s plus 12. Pure water contributes volume but no salt, so adding a salt term for it, as option B does, invents salt that was never there. Forgetting the 12 litres of water in the total volume would make the equation describe a weaker mixture than the one asked for.
questions.hint: Write salt in equals salt out, and let the water contribute volume only.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: solve a mixture equation for the amount of one component
questions.stem: How many litres of a 40 percent salt solution must be added to 12 litres of pure water so that the result is a 20 percent solution? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Letting x be the litres of the 40 percent solution, the salt balance is 0.4x equal to 0.2 of the quantity x plus 12, which gives 0.2x equal to 2.4 and x equal to 12. The reason is easy to see afterwards: 12 litres of a 40 percent solution holds 4.8 litres of salt, and with 12 litres of water the total is 24 litres, so 4.8 in 24 is exactly 20 percent. Adding the salt of the water to both sides, or leaving the extra 12 litres out of the total volume, would each describe a different mixture from the one asked for.
questions.hint: Equate the salt brought in with the salt in the final volume.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: solve a system by substitution and confirm it by elimination
questions.stem: A system reads 5x plus 4y equal to 26 together with y equals 2x minus 1. Solving it, what is the value of y? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Replacing y with 2x minus 1 gives 5x plus 8x minus 4 equal to 26, so 13x equal to 30 and x equal to 30 over 13, which gives y equal to 60 over 13 minus 1, that is 47 over 13. Elimination agrees: the second equation rewritten as 2x minus y equal to 1, tripled to give 6x minus 3y equal to 3 and added to the first, leaves 11x equal to 29, which matches the same value of x. Both equations then check, since 5 times 30 over 13 plus 4 times 47 over 13 is 150 over 13 plus 188 over 13, which is 338 over 13, equal to 26.
questions.hint: Replace the variable that stands alone with its rule, then confirm with a second method.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Distance where two plans cost the same
questions.learningObjective: solve for the input where two cost rules agree
questions.stem: One ride service charges a fixed 6 dollars plus 0.50 dollars for each kilometre, while a rival charges a flat 21 dollars for any journey of any length. For what distance in kilometres do the two charges agree? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Setting the two charges equal gives 6 plus 0.5d equal to 21, so 0.5d is 15 and d is 15 divided by 0.5, which is 30 kilometres. The check is to run that distance through both prices: 0.5 times 30 is 15, and 6 plus 15 is 21, exactly the flat fare. The trap is treating 0.50 as 5 when dividing, which would give a distance of 3 instead.
questions.hint: Find the distance charge that makes the total reach 21 dollars, then divide.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Rate of change as a slope
questions.learningObjective: read a slope as a rate of change with its units
questions.stem: A delivery log records distance in kilometres against time in hours at the points 0 and 0, 2 and 50, 4 and 100, and 6 and 150. What does the slope of this line represent?

options.text: The distance covered in the first hour, which the slope never fixes
options.misconception: believes a rate of change describes only the opening interval

options.text: A stopping time of about 0.04 hours per kilometre as time moves right
options.misconception: inverts the ratio and then calls the result a speed

options.text: A total journey length of 150 kilometres reached at the last point shown
options.misconception: reads the last plotted value as the meaning of the slope

options.text: A steady speed of 25 kilometres per hour, as the time moves right

questions.explanation: A slope is a rate of change, and here the distance rises by 50 kilometres for every 2 hours of travel, which is 25 kilometres per hour, the speed the van holds throughout. Putting distance over time gives the speed, and reversing the ratio would give hours per kilometre, a measure of how long each kilometre takes rather than how fast the van is going. The last plotted value is only a reading at one moment and says nothing about the rate.
questions.hint: Divide the change in distance by the change in time, keeping the units in that order.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: convert units before reporting a rate per second
questions.stem: A cutting machine advances 4.5 metres of pipe in every 8 seconds of running time. How many centimetres per second does that correspond to? Report the number to the nearest hundredth.
questions.explanation: A rate needs its units to match the question, so the 4.5 metres is first rewritten as 450 centimetres, and 450 divided by 8 is 56.25 centimetres per second. Working the other way round gives the same figure: 4.5 divided by 8 is 0.5625 metres per second, and multiplying that by 100 to reach centimetres returns 56.25. Converting after dividing, or forgetting the factor of 100 entirely, produces a rate that is off by two orders of magnitude.
questions.hint: Convert the distance to centimetres first, then divide by the seconds.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: apply a constant of proportionality found from one known pair
questions.stem: A courier charges in proportion to the mass carried, and a 6 kilogram consignment costs 42 dollars. How much does a 10 kilogram consignment cost under the same rate? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The constant of proportionality is the dollars per kilogram, and 42 divided by 6 is 7, so 10 kilograms costs 10 times 7, which is 70 dollars. The check runs the other way: 70 divided by 10 is 7, the same rate as before, which is the test a proportional relationship must pass. Scaling from 6 to 10 by a factor of 5 over 3 and applying that to 42 gives the same 70, and forgetting to scale the cost as well as the mass is the usual slip.
questions.hint: Find the dollars per kilogram from the known pair, then multiply it by 10.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Extending a model past the data
questions.learningObjective: name the assumption a linear model needs when it is used beyond the data
questions.stem: A box office sold 40, then 55, then 70 tickets on three successive weekends, and a student fits the rule y equal to 40 plus 15 times x, where x counts weekends from the first. What must hold for the rule to be used at the tenth weekend?

options.text: The tenth weekend is near enough that the rule must be exact there
options.misconception: believes closeness to the data guarantees the answer is right

options.text: The gain of 15 tickets each weekend must carry on, unchanged and without limit
Sales must begin falling by 15 tickets a weekend past the third
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the trend when extending the rule

options.text: The recorded total of 165 tickets must cap the sales at any weekend
options.misconception: treats a sum of past values as a hard ceiling on the future

questions.explanation: Three increasing values do not prove that the increase will keep the same size, so using the rule at the tenth weekend is a claim that the constant 15 ticket gain continues unchanged, which is exactly the assumption that has to be tested. Distance from the data is not evidence, and reversing the trend or imposing a ceiling would each contradict the rule that was fitted. A model fitted to a short record is a statement about what has happened so far, and extending it adds an assumption rather than a deduction.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule assumes about the future, not what the three points show.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Answer ruled out by the context
questions.learningObjective: reject a model answer that the context makes impossible
questions.stem: A model of spare seats on a minibus, built for small numbers of passengers, reports negative 6 seats for a bus carrying 45 passengers. Which conclusion about that report is sound?

options.text: The model is right, and 45 passengers should be removed from the count
options.misconception: edits the data so that a broken model appears to work

options.text: The bus truly needs negative 6 seats, which a large credit could cover
options.misconception: accepts an impossible count because the model produced it

options.text: The model does not reach this far, because a seat count cannot be negative
The figure 39 is the right answer, obtained by adding 45 to the output
options.misconception: patches a wrong output with arithmetic instead of questioning the model

questions.explanation: A model is built for a range of situations, and a number that cannot exist in the real world is the clearest possible evidence that the situation lies outside that range, so the report is rejected rather than repaired. Adding 45 to reach 39, or removing passengers until the output looks reasonable, both keep a model that has already given itself away. Checking the sign and the size of a result against the context costs nothing and catches a wrong method before it becomes a wrong answer.
questions.hint: Ask whether a count of that kind can exist before asking whether the arithmetic worked.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: System of equations from a word problem
questions.learningObjective: translate two conditions into a system and solve for a single unknown
questions.stem: Two numbers add to 24, and the larger is twice the smaller. What is the larger number? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: If the smaller number is x, the larger is 2x and the total is 3x equal to 24, so x equal to 8 and the larger number is 16. The check is that 8 plus 16 is 24 and that 16 is twice 8, so both conditions hold. Solving 24 equal to 2x gives 12, which is the value the smaller number would take if the larger were not twice it.
questions.hint: Name the smaller number, express the larger as twice it, then use the total sum.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Perpendicular line through a given point
questions.learningObjective: build the line through a point with the slope perpendicular to a given line
questions.stem: A cable runs along the line y equals 2x plus 5, and a brace must cross it at a right angle at the point where x is 2 and y is 9. What is the vertical intercept of the brace? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The brace slope is the negative reciprocal of 2, which is negative one half, and substituting the point 2 and 9 into y equals negative one half of x plus b gives 9 equal to negative 1 plus b, so b equal to 10. Keeping the original intercept of 5, keeping the original slope, or reversing the sign without the reciprocal each fail one of the two conditions. The slope product check and the point-substitution check are what confirm the answer.
questions.hint: Take the negative reciprocal of the slope, then choose the constant to hit the point.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why a vertical line has an undefined slope
questions.stem: The graph of the equation x equals 11 is a single vertical column. What is the slope of that column, and what is the reason?

options.text: Undefined, because a slope exists only for a line through the origin
options.misconception: ties the undefined slope to where a line sits rather than which way it runs

options.text: Zero, because the column runs up and down while staying in one file
options.misconception: describes the behaviour of a horizontal line and assigns it to a vertical one

options.text: Eleven, because the line holds the fixed value of 11 for every input
options.misconception: reads the constant in the equation as the slope of the column

options.text: Undefined, because along the column x never changes while y does change

questions.explanation: A slope is rise divided by run, and along a vertical column the run is zero while the rise is not, so the quotient is undefined rather than zero. Zero would be the honest answer for a horizontal line, where the rise is zero and the run is not, and that is exactly the pair of options most often confused. The origin has nothing to do with it: a vertical column anywhere has this property, and its equation simply has no y term to rearrange.
questions.hint: Ask how much the input changes as you travel along the column.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: connect the parallel condition to a system with no solution
questions.stem: A system has two equations in standard form whose left sides are multiples of each other, but the right-hand sides are not multiples in the same ratio. What can be said about the system before any solving is done?

options.text: It has one solution, because the two equations were written with different constants
options.misconception: believes unequal constants always yield a crossing for any pair of lines

options.text: It has no solution, because the two lines are parallel and never meet
It has infinitely many solutions, because the two left sides match in ratio
options.misconception: scores proportionality of the left sides while the right sides stay apart

options.text: It cannot be judged from the coefficients alone, so the equations must be solved
options.misconception: believes the coefficients are useless for deciding a system's outcome

questions.explanation: When the left sides are proportional but the constants are not, the two equations have the same slope and different intercepts, which describes parallel lines with no common point. The ratio of the constants is the decisive detail, since a matching ratio there would make the two equations the same line and the solution set infinite. Judging from the coefficients first saves work, and it also explains why solving by elimination would produce a false statement.
questions.hint: Check whether the constant on the right scales by the same factor as the whole left side.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: System with one solution from two non-parallel lines
questions.learningObjective: solve a system whose two lines cross exactly once
questions.stem: A solver is handed three systems and reports one answer per system: system A returns a single pair, system B returns the message that nothing satisfies it, and system C returns the message that every point of one line works. Which claim orders the three correctly?

options.text: A is two crossing lines, B is two copies of one line, and C is two parallel lines
options.misconception: swaps the messages given for coincident and parallel lines

options.text: A is two parallel lines, B is two crossing lines, and C is two copies of one line
options.misconception: swaps the messages given for parallel and crossing lines

options.text: A is two crossing lines, B is two parallel lines, and C is two copies of one line
A is two copies of one line, B is two crossing lines, and C is two parallel lines
options.misconception: reads the single answer as a sign of coincident lines rather than a crossing

questions.explanation: A single solution is exactly a pair of lines that cross once, an empty solution set is a parallel pair, and an infinite solution set is a pair that are really the same line. The pictures and the algebra messages match, which is why the solver's output can be read as a description of the lines. Swapping any two of the messages pairs the wrong geometry with the wrong algebra.
questions.hint: Match each solver message with the geometry that produces it.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an elimination step that dropped a term
questions.stem: A student solves 3x plus 4y equal to 20 and 5x minus 4y equal to 8 by adding the equations and writing 8x equal to 28, then reports x equal to 3.5. Where is the error in that working?

options.text: The student should have divided 20 by 4 first, since the 4 belongs to both sides
options.misconception: divides terms inside an equation that is to be combined, not rearranged

options.text: The y terms should have been subtracted rather than added, since they carry opposite signs
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the combination that already cancels a variable

options.text: The x coefficients should have been matched before the equations were combined
options.misconception: adds a scaling requirement where none is needed once one variable cancels

options.text: The right sides must be added too, giving 8x equal to 28 only if 20 plus 8 is 28, which it is

questions.explanation: Adding the two equations cancels the y terms and gives 8x equal to 28, since 20 plus 8 is 28, so the working is actually sound and x equal to 3.5 is correct. The value of y then comes from substituting back, giving 4y equal to 9.5 and y equal to 2.375, which satisfies both equations. Reviewing claimed errors without checking the arithmetic first is the trap here, since the step that looks suspicious can be perfectly legal.
questions.hint: Check the arithmetic of the claimed error before accepting that an error exists.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: System with no solution in context
questions.learningObjective: recognise an impossible system in a real situation
questions.stem: Two printing firms quote the same price list in different forms: firm A states 3 dollars per poster plus a flat 12 dollars, and firm B states 3 dollars per poster plus a flat 15 dollars. A planner sets the two quotes equal. What outcome should the planner expect?

options.text: One number of posters makes the quotes agree, found by dividing 3 by the 12 and 15
options.misconception: divides two constants and calls the quotient a matching quantity

options.text: No number of posters makes the quotes agree, because the per poster rates match and the fees differ
Every number of posters makes the quotes agree, because the per poster rates are the same
options.misconception: reads a shared rate as a shared total rather than a shared direction

options.text: The planner cannot know, because both firms may add hidden charges later
options.misconception: treats an unwritten contingency as the reason a stated system has no solution

questions.explanation: With the same per poster rate on both sides, cancelling posters leaves 12 equal to 15, which is false, so no quantity can make the two quotes agree. The two quotes are parallel cost rules that stay 3 dollars apart forever, and the planner should read that as firm A always being cheaper. A shared rate never makes the totals agree unless the fixed fees agree too, which is the condition the second option misses.
questions.hint: Cancel the parts that match and read the number statement that is left.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Graphs of a system with one solution
questions.learningObjective: read the number of solutions from the shape of two graphs
questions.stem: Two graphs are drawn on one grid. One rises by 2 for each unit across and the other falls by 3 for each unit across. What can be said about the system they represent?

options.text: The system has infinitely many solutions, since both graphs are straight lines
options.misconception: assumes every pair of straight lines on one grid is the same line

options.text: The system has no solution, since the two graphs move in opposite directions
options.misconception: believes lines moving in opposite directions never meet

options.text: The system has exactly one solution, since rising and falling lines must cross
The system has two solutions, one for each of the two graphs on the grid
options.misconception: counts one solution for each equation rather than shared points

questions.explanation: Two lines with different slopes, and here one rises while the other falls, cannot be parallel and cannot coincide, so they cross exactly once. That single crossing point is the solution of the system, because it lies on both graphs. Lines moving in opposite directions still meet unless they have the same slope, and two straight lines are the same only when both slope and intercept agree.
questions.hint: Compare the slopes of the two graphs before counting any points.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: estimate a solution from a graph and refine it algebraically
questions.stem: Two rules are y equals 3x plus 1 and y equals x plus 9. Setting the two rules equal gives the solution of the system. What is the value of x? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Setting the two rules equal gives 3x plus 1 equal to x plus 9, so 2x equal to 8 and x equal to 4. The output is then 13, and both rules check, since 3 times 4 plus 1 is 13 and 4 plus 9 is 13. Subtracting x from only one side, or moving the 9 to the left without changing its sign, are the two slips that give a different value.
questions.hint: Put the two right-hand sides equal, then collect the x terms on one side.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: convert a repeating increase into a rate per unit time
questions.stem: Snow settles on a roof at a steady rate, rising 3 centimetres every 6 minutes. What is the rate of rise in centimetres per minute? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The rate is the rise over the time, so 3 divided by 6 is 0.5 centimetres each minute, and the same figure appears if the whole ratio is written in larger units as 30 millimetres over 60 minutes, which is again 0.5. Putting the minutes on top would give the time taken per centimetre, which is 2 and answers a different question. A steady rate like this is exactly what makes the relationship proportional, since each equal interval adds an equal amount.
questions.hint: Divide the height gained by the minutes it took to gain it.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: System with infinitely many solutions in context
questions.learningObjective: explain why two descriptions of one line give infinitely many solutions
questions.stem: A shop records the same stock rule twice, once as 2x plus 6y equal to 24 and once as x plus 3y equal to 12. A clerk asks whether solving this system will produce one pair of stock numbers. What is the answer?

options.text: No, because two records of one rule can never be solved together at all
options.misconception: believes a repeated rule is unsolvable rather than infinitely satisfied

options.text: Yes, because the two records were written with different coefficients on the left
options.misconception: believes different-looking left sides always produce a distinct line

options.text: Yes, because the right sides 24 and 12 differ and force a single stock pair
options.misconception: reads a constant difference as the source of a unique solution

options.text: No, because the second record is half the first, so one line is described and all its points satisfy both

questions.explanation: Every term of the second record, constant included, is half of the first, so both records describe exactly the same set of points and the system is satisfied by every point of that one line. A system produces a single pair only when the two equations describe lines with different slopes. Writing the same rule twice is not an error to work around, it is the dependent case that produces infinitely many solutions.
questions.hint: Compare the two records term by term, including the constant on the right.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how a vertical line affects a system's solution
questions.stem: A system contains the vertical line x equals 5 together with the sloped line y equals 2x plus 3. How many solutions does the system have?

options.text: None at all, since the vertical line has no slope to match against the other
options.misconception: believes an undefined slope keeps a line from ever crossing another

options.text: Exactly one, since a vertical line meets a non-vertical line in a single point
Infinitely many, since the sloped line passes through every height above the vertical one
options.misconception: mistakes a line covering every height for one covering every point

options.text: Exactly two, because each equation lists a different coordinate pair for the meeting point
options.misconception: expects two equations to yield two separate points of agreement

questions.explanation: A vertical line cuts any non-vertical line exactly once, so the system has one solution, found by substituting 5 into the sloped rule to get the output 13. The undefined slope of the vertical line prevents slope comparisons with the parallel and perpendicular rules, but it does not stop the two lines from crossing. Infinitely many solutions would require the two lines to be the same, which a vertical and a sloped line can never be.
questions.hint: Substitute the fixed value of x into the sloped rule and find the output.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Answer that makes sense in a system
questions.learningObjective: reject a fractional answer where a whole count is required
questions.stem: A system built from a stall-holder problem gives 6.5 for the number of adult passes sold. Which response to that result is sound?

options.text: Round it to 7, on the grounds that rounding down never overstates a count
options.misconception: rounds in one fixed direction instead of finding the fault

options.text: Round it to 8, since a whole number is wanted and 7.5 is nearer 8
options.misconception: hides a wrong setup behind a rounding step

options.text: Set it aside and check the setup, since a count of tickets is a whole number
Accept 7.5, since part tickets can be booked for a family party
options.misconception: stretches the meaning of the context to fit an impossible count

questions.explanation: Half a ticket is not a quantity that exists, so the number cannot be right, and the useful question is which part of the setup is at fault rather than how to tidy the output. Rounding in either direction invents a data point that the problem never contained, and claiming that part tickets are sold stretches the context to fit an impossible result. A quick check of kind, sign and size against the words of the problem is a habit worth building, since it catches a bad equation before the arithmetic is even finished.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of quantity the answer should be before asking what it equals.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solving a system with a parameter
questions.learningObjective: solve a system whose right-hand sides contain a parameter
questions.stem: A system reads 2x plus 3y equal to 8 together with 4x plus 6y equal to 16, and a student reports that it has no solution because doubling the first equation gives the second. What is the error in that reading?

options.text: The system is unsolvable because the variable terms double along with the constant
options.misconception: treats a consistent scaling of every term as a sign of inconsistency

options.text: The student should have looked at the different coefficients of x before deciding anything
options.misconception: compares unequal-looking coefficients when one equation is a multiple of the other

options.text: The system has exactly one solution, because the two equations hold different information
options.misconception: assumes two differently written equations must yield a single pair

options.text: Both sides double exactly, so the equations describe the same line and the solution set is infinite

questions.explanation: Doubling every term of the first equation gives exactly the second, so the two equations are not two different conditions but one written twice, and the solution set is the whole line. That is why eliminating produces the true statement 0 equal to 0 rather than a false one. The error is treating an equation that looks different as a new constraint, which is the same mistake as reading a scaled left side while ignoring the scaled right side.
questions.hint: Double every term of the first equation and compare it with the second one.

questions.topic: Solution count of a system in context

options.text: No quantity makes the two prices match, because the per unit rates are equal and the fees are not

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Using a linear rule beyond the data
questions.learningObjective: apply a fitted linear rule for a year beyond the recorded range
questions.stem: A club had 30 members in 2020 and gained 4 members every year after that, and a student uses the rule y equal to 30 plus 4x, where x counts years since 2020. What does the rule give for 2027? Report the number only.

Counting the gains one at a time reaches the same place: 34 after one year, 38 after two, and so on up to 58 after seven, which is a good check because it never needs the rule at all. The assumption being made is that the gain of 4 a year continues, since nothing in the recorded observations can guarantee what happens years later.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solving a system by substitution with negatives
questions.learningObjective: solve a system whose substitution involves negative numbers
questions.stem: A system given for a temperature model reads 3x plus 2y equal to 1 together with y equals negative 4. Solving it, what is the value of x? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Replacing y with negative 4 gives 3x minus 8 equal to 1, so 3x equal to 9 and x equal to 3. The check is that 9 plus 2 times negative 4 is 9 minus 8, which is 1, so the pair satisfies the first equation and the second one trivially. Adding 8 instead of subtracting it when the y term is moved, or dividing 1 by 3 without isolating x, are the slips that give a different value.
questions.hint: Replace the variable that stands alone with its value, then solve the remaining equation.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: choose the scaling that makes two coefficients cancel
questions.stem: In the system 2x plus 9y equals 16 and 4x minus 3y equals 14, by what factor must the second equation be multiplied so that the y terms cancel when the equations are added? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The y coefficients are 9 and negative 3, so tripling the second equation brings its coefficient to negative 9 and lets the two equations be added to cancel y. Doubling or scaling the first equation leaves the 9 unmatched, and adding as they stand combines the coefficients rather than cancelling them. The smallest shared size for the two coefficients is 9, and reaching it requires a factor of 3 on the second equation.
questions.hint: Find the smallest number into which both y coefficients can be scaled.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Graphing a system to count its solutions
questions.learningObjective: use the slope and intercept of each rule to predict the solution count
questions.stem: A plot prints two lines and labels them with their rules. The first is y equals 0.5x plus 3 and the second is y equals 0.5x plus 3, plus a note that the second was scaled up by a factor of 2 on both sides. What does the system contain?

options.text: Two crossing lines, because the second equation is a different multiple of the first
options.misconception: thinks a multiple of an equation must be a different line

options.text: Two parallel lines, because scaling a rule changes where its line sits on the grid
options.misconception: believes multiplying both sides of an equation moves its line

options.text: A single line drawn twice, because scaling both sides of a rule leaves the line unchanged
No lines at all, because a scaled rule cannot be graphed on the same grid
options.misconception: believes a scaled equation is meaningless on the same axes

questions.explanation: Multiplying every term of an equation by the same non-zero number describes the same set of points, so the two rules place one line on the grid twice and the system has infinitely many solutions. Scaling an equation changes its appearance, not its meaning, which is why elimination can rely on it. A different multiple of one equation becomes a parallel line only when the constant is scaled by a different factor, which the plot does not report.
questions.hint: Ask whether doubling both sides of an equation could change any point on its graph.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: use the perpendicular condition to judge a system's crossing angle
questions.stem: A system reads 4x minus 2y equal to 6 and x plus 2y equal to 5. Which statement about the two graphs of this system is correct?

options.text: They cross at an acute angle, since both slopes carry a nonzero magnitude
options.misconception: assumes any two nonzero slopes must meet other than at a right angle

options.text: They are parallel, since the second equation is a fraction of the first one
options.misconception: reads a different arrangement of the coefficients as the same slope

options.text: They are the same line, since both equations contain a plus 2y term
options.misconception: matches one term in each equation and calls the lines identical

options.text: They cross at a right angle, since their slopes are 2 and negative one half

questions.explanation: Isolating y gives the slopes 2 and negative one half, and their product is negative 1, so the two lines cross at a right angle, which also means the system has exactly one solution. Parallel lines would need equal slopes, and identical lines would need both slope and intercept to match. The presence of a right angle does not remove the solution; it describes the angle at the single crossing point.
questions.hint: Isolate the output in each equation, then multiply the two slopes.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solving a system in a real context
questions.learningObjective: solve a two-equation system stated with two unknown totals
questions.stem: A bakery sells loaves at 3 dollars each and buns at 2 dollars each. One day the till showed 18 dollars and 7 items were sold. How many loaves were sold? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Letting l be loaves gives buns as 7 minus l, and the money equation is 3l plus 2 times the quantity 7 minus l equal to 18, so l equal to 4. Then buns equal to 3, and both checks hold: 4 plus 3 is 7 items, and 12 plus 6 is 18 dollars. Attaching the prices to the wrong item, or forgetting that the two counts must add to 7, gives a pair that fails one of the conditions.
questions.hint: Write one equation for the number of items and one for the money, then substitute.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solution count of a system after elimination
questions.learningObjective: read the solution count from the statement left after elimination
questions.stem: Eliminating a variable from a system leaves the statement 5 equal to 5. Which conclusion about the system follows directly?

options.text: The system has no solution, because eliminating a variable cannot produce a solution
options.misconception: believes an eliminated variable means nothing can satisfy the system

options.text: The system has infinitely many solutions, because nothing is left to restrict the variable
The system has exactly one solution, because 5 is a single number on both sides
options.misconception: reads a true constant statement as a single value of the solution

options.text: The system has exactly five solutions, because the statement names the number 5
options.misconception: reads the numeral in the leftover statement as a count of solutions

questions.explanation: When every variable cancels and the statement left is true, the second equation adds nothing the first one did not already say, so the two equations describe the same line and every point of it is a solution. A false statement would instead give an empty solution set, and a remaining variable would give a single pair. The numeral in the leftover statement is part of the truth, never a count of answers.
questions.hint: Ask whether the leftover statement is true or false, and whether any variable remains.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: read a value off a graph that extends past the plotted points
questions.stem: A revenue line is graphed from the points where units are 0 and revenue is 0, and units are 5 and revenue is 45. What does the graph give for revenue at 12 units? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The line rises 45 over 5 units, which is 9 per unit, so at 12 units the revenue is 12 times 9, which is 108. Building the rule confirms it, since the line passes through the origin and the slope is 9, giving 108 at the input 12. Reading the revenue off the nearest plotted point instead of extending the line gives 45, which is the value at 5 units and not at 12.
questions.hint: Find the slope from the two plotted points, then evaluate the rule at 12 units.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: System of two plans that never meet
questions.learningObjective: identify an inconsistent pair of plans in a table
questions.stem: Two insurance plans quote an annual cost in dollars against a deductible in dollars. Plan A costs 2 times the deductible plus 100, and Plan B costs 2 times the deductible plus 150. What does the table of these quotes show?

options.text: The plans agree at every deductible, because both double the same amount
options.misconception: reads a shared coefficient as a shared total for both plans

options.text: The plans agree at 25 dollars of deductible, found by dividing 50 by 2
options.misconception: divides a constant difference by a coefficient that cancels

options.text: Plan B is always 50 dollars dearer, because the two rules are parallel
The plans agree at 100 dollars, because that is the value Plan A starts from
options.misconception: reports an intercept as a point of agreement between two rules

questions.explanation: Both rules carry the same coefficient of 2, so cancelling the deductible leaves 100 equal to 150, which is false, and the two cost rules are parallel lines that stay 50 dollars apart at every deductible. No choice of deductible can close a gap that the algebra removes entirely. Dividing 50 by 2 divides a difference that has never been matched by a variable on the other side.
questions.hint: Set the two cost rules equal and read the number statement that survives.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solving a system for a variable after substitution
questions.learningObjective: solve a system and report one of the two values
questions.stem: A system reads x plus 4y equal to 25 together with y equal to x minus 5. Solving it, what is the value of y? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Replacing y with x minus 5 gives x plus 4x minus 20 equal to 25, so 5x equal to 45 and x equal to 9. Then y equal to 4, and both equations check, since 9 plus 16 is 25 and 4 is indeed 9 minus 5. Substituting in the wrong direction, so that x stands for the rule for y, produces a pair that fails one of the two equations.
questions.hint: Replace the variable that stands alone with its rule, then solve for the other one.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: compare a line of positive slope with a line of negative slope
questions.stem: A train schedule graphs passengers against hours for two services. The first rises steadily and the second falls steadily, and both graphs are straight lines. Which claim about the two services is sound?

options.text: The two graphs cross twice, once for each service on the same grid
options.misconception: expects one crossing for each line rather than one shared point

options.text: The two graphs never cross, because they move in opposite directions
options.misconception: believes lines moving in opposite directions never meet on a grid

options.text: The two graphs run parallel, because both are straight lines on one grid
options.misconception: assumes any two straight lines on one grid are parallel

options.text: The two graphs cross once, because one slope is positive and the other is negative

questions.explanation: A rising line has a positive slope and a falling line has a negative slope, so the two cannot be parallel and cannot coincide, which forces exactly one crossing point. That point is where the two services carry the same number of passengers, and it is the solution of the system made by the two rules. Two straight lines are parallel only when their slopes are equal, which is not the case here.
questions.hint: Compare the signs of the two slopes before counting crossings.
